https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-polls-22503108.php
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging.
In early October, a Politico poll found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop.
40, while 43% planned to vote no, with the rest undecided, essentially the same finding as it had a month earlier.

Californians’ appetite for a first-in-the-nation wealth tax appears to be waning.
With less than a week before Election Day, support for Proposition 40, a proposed billionaire tax, is now under water, according to the latest poll by Public Policy Institute of California.
Published Tuesday, the survey found that 46% of 1,086 likely voters support the tax, while 52% don’t.
That’s a notable change from last month, when Prop.
40 proponents held a slim 52% majority.
The billionaire tax is by far the biggest and most expensive fight on the ballot.

Meanwhile, a pair of related ballot measures intended to negate the billionaire tax could go either way.

# California billionaires tax trails in another poll days before election
## The Berkeley IGS survey finds 50% oppose Proposition 40 and 42% support it. Two measures aimed at blocking the tax also lack majority support.

**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...**
California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed, with 8% undecided.
In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided.
It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided.
Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass.

The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.

I'm weighing the voter mood against the electorate: the sour mood could drag down bond support, but the heavy Democratic turnout, with Becerra up 24 to 27 points, points to a leaning that favors Prop 1. I'm also checking the base rate, since most California statewide bonds since 2000 have passed, with a handful of notable failures.

I'm going back through the past California bond results, where legislative bonds in general elections have nearly always passed, and the exceptions have been initiatives or primary contests. I'm also looking at what PPIC's polling said before the 2018 and 2020 bond votes, since the pre-election numbers were not a clean predictor of the final results.

I'm recalling how PPIC's October bond polling compared with the final results: the March 2024 Prop 1 and the November 2024 school and climate bonds. The October numbers for those bonds look reasonably predictive, so I'm treating that pattern as a useful guide.

I'm reading the 60-38 October number as a strong sign Prop 1 will pass, given the lack of organized opposition and the $15M behind it. I'll still check for late opposition, like a Howard Jarvis campaign, and weigh whether the sour mood and the crowded bond ballot, with Prop 37 and Prop 38, could create bond fatigue. The polls show all of them with majority support, so I'll look at the AIMSA details next.

Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)
10/28/2026 09:00 AM EDT

Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.

IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.
LOS ANGELES
Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.

By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)

Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman

Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
By JEREMY B. WHITE (https://www.politico.com/staff/jeremy-b-white), BLAKE JONES (https://www.politico.com/staff/blake-jones) and MELANIE MASON (https://www.politico.com/staff/melanie-mason)

Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.

TOP READS
SHATTERED RECORDS — Billionaire opponents of California’s proposed wealth tax have spent more fighting it than they ever have on a political cause in the state, according to a POLITICO analysis.
A record $612 million from more than 70 current and former California billionaires is flooding this year’s state elections , nearly half of it to groups working to defeat the wealth tax initiative on Tuesday’s ballot, POLITICO found.
The fight over Prop 40 has brought California’s wealthiest residents — many from its native tech industry — together in an unprecedented show of political coordination, the new data reveals. Tech leaders say the wealth tax has accelerated plans for broader political engagement this cycle, building networks that could be the foundation for future campaigns.
Read the full story from Christine Mui and Sean McMinn here (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/28/billionaires-spending-california-wealth-tax-01137778) .
IN THE COURTS
In this Aug. 30, 2021, file photo, mail-in ballots run through a sorting machine at the Sacramento County Registrar of Voters office in Sacramento, California. | Rich Pedroncelli/AP
ELECTION CLAIM SKEPTIC — A federal judge in California signaled Tuesday that he is preparing to reject the Trump administration’s emergency effort to force the state to set aside and review any votes cast by people on a list of 20,000 registered voters the Department of Homeland Security has identified as likely noncitizens.
After a three-hour hearing, U.S. District Judge David Carter instead said he needed a far more extensive briefing on the matter that would extend well past Election Day. In effect, it’s a defeat for the Justice Department, which had demanded the judge immediately force the state to comply. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said DOJ could prosecute anyone it identifies as casting an illegal ballot.
“Of course no one wants a noncitizen voting. Anybody taking that position, it’s a ridiculous position,” he said.
The judge concluded with a stark warning for DOJ, however, after state officials complained that the Trump administration had made menacing comments about potentially prosecuting election workers who tabulated the votes of noncitizens: “This court believes it would be wise that any threats to state and county elected employees cease immediately.”
Carter said he would issue a formal order Wednesday. — Kyle Cheney
First Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks during an announcement at Department of Justice headquarters in Washington on Nov. 19, 2025. | Francis Chung/POLITICO
WHAT’S IN A NAME — A federal judge ruled Tuesday that Bill Essayli is unlawfully acting as a “de facto” U.S. attorney.
Judge J. Michael Seabright , who last year ruled that Essayli was illegally serving in the role (https://www.politico.com/news/2025/10/28/judge-los-angeles-top-federal-prosecutor-illegally-appointed-00626804) of acting U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, wrote that “Essayli—even in his designated role as a Special Attorney and FAUSA—is disqualified from (1) participating in or supervising these cases, or (2) otherwise supervising any attorneys in the handling of these cases.”
Essayli said in a statement that he respectfully disagreed with the ruling.
“The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department,” he said.
Essayli added that the motion was automatically stayed, and that the status quo will likely remain while the DOJ appeals the decision. “Ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court,” he said, “and I look forward to serving in my current role until then.” — Nicole Norman
ELECTION YEAR
Chad Bianco speaks during a California gubernatorial debate hosted by CBS Bay Area and the San Francisco Examiner in San Francisco, Thursday, May 14, 2026. | Godofredo A. Vásquez/AP
RELUCTANT SUPPORT? — It was hardly a ringing endorsement, but Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco , who previously declined to endorse (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) Steve Hilton in the governor’s race after losing the primary, voiced support for his fellow Republican’s candidacy on Tuesday.
“I don’t care if you like him or not. We absolutely need Steve Hilton to win this race for governor,” Bianco said in a video on social media (https://x.com/ChadBianco/status/2115188593425850374?a=NXWO74gQaasvSVU-EC4&s=20).
Bianco in May argued (https://www.fresnobee.com/news/politics-government/article315864431.html) that President Donald Trump ’s endorsement of Hilton (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/04/06/before-trump-backed-hilton-loomer-was-already-at-work-00861205) would hurt the former Fox News host in California. But he urged followers to vote for Hilton in the video, anyway, saying “we need balance” amid Democratic rule.
IN THE PHONE BANK — Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas rallied volunteers at a phone bank supporting Democrat Amy Slavensky , telling them her incumbent opponent Assemblymember Josh Hoover is a “nice guy, but he doesn’t represent this community’s interests.” Outgoing Women’s Caucus Chair Cecilia Aguiar-Curry said electing Slavensky, a former school administrator, was a priority of the caucus. And Assemblymember Gail Pellerin , a former local elections official, instructed callers to encourage voters to drop off their ballots in person rather than by mail, citing concerns about possible Trump administration interference.
“We cannot rely on the United States Postal Service right now because they are under the control of this Trump administration, and we don’t want those ballots to get held somewhere and not in the hands of the elections official,” Pellerin told the volunteers gathered in the Sacramento suburb of Fair Oaks.
The event’s attendance by several Democratic officials, including Assemblymember Patrick Ahrens , underscored the force with which their party is trying to oust Hoover despite his moderate profile and, as Rivas seemed to acknowledge, affable demeanor. The state Democratic Party has poured more than $2 million into defeating the frontline Republican, one of several incumbents it’s trying to oust after losing seats in both chambers of the Legislature last cycle.
Super PACs, including the GOP caucus-aligned Legislative Action Victory PAC and another sponsored by CalChamber, have collectively spent more than $3 million defending Hoover and blasting Slavensky.

Los Angeles mayoral candidate Nithya Raman speaks during a campaign event on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026, in Sylmar, California. | William Liang/AP
POWER PLAY — Frustration over sky-high electricity bills is becoming a flashpoint in the closing days of the Los Angeles mayor’s race, with Karen Bass and her progressive challenger, Nithya Raman , trading blows over utility costs that have soared amid record-breaking heatwaves, Alex Nieves reports for subscribers (https://subscriber.politicopro.com/article/2026/10/the-la-mayors-race-goes-electric-01137758).
The fracas began early last week after Raman held a press conference alongside frustrated Los Angeles Department of Water and Power customers, where the council member blamed Bass for letting the utility raise electricity and water rates without City Council approval — and promised to audit the department. Bass has responded with promises to lower bills and investigate the city’s climbing utility costs.
The last-minute brawl comes as candidates statewide contend with high electricity prices and broader concerns about the cost of living — an issue (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) which is among voters’ top concerns. California’s electricity rates are the second-highest in the U.S., behind only Hawaii. Read last night’s California Currents (https://www.politico.com/newsletters/california-currents/2026/10/27/ramans-electric-closing-message-01137445) to see how both campaigns are trying to navigate energy affordability angst ahead of Election Day.

# America's Housing Crisis Is on the Ballot This Election Day
## California Voters Face 3 Housing Proposals
In California, 32.6% of the state’s homeowners spend at least 30% of their income on housing, the largest share nationwide.
Among renters, 55.5% spend 30% or more of their income on housing, the third largest share.
Proposition 1 is a referendum that would authorize the state to issue bonds of up to $11.25 billion to fund affordable rental housing and homeownership assistance programs.
If approved, $7.2 billion would be spent to buy, build or renovate an estimated 40,000 rental units, largely through low-interest loans to developers.
Some projects would have to reserve units for low-income households and for homeless people.
Approval would also dedicate $1.25 billion to help military veterans with loans to buy homes, while hundreds of millions of dollars would fund improvements to infrastructure needed for housing, farmworker housing and housing grants for Native American tribes.
The measures within Proposition 1 were approved by California’s Democrat-dominated state senate in June 2026, but the amount of bond debt that must be incurred to pay for them means that voters will have the final say.

PROP 1: The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%201.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 (SB 417, Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026, Limón).
Type: Legislative referral (general obligation bond act). Placed by the legislature, not by citizen signatures.
A vote YES means: The state may borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds. This includes about $10 billion in general obligation bonds that would fund affordable housing construction, rehabilitation, and homeownership programs, repaid from the general fund, and about $1.25 billion in revenue bonds funding CalVet home loans, repaid by the veterans who borrow.
A vote NO means: The state does not authorize this borrowing. Existing state housing programs continue with whatever money remains from prior bonds and the annual budget.
Sponsor/proponent: Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón (lead Senate author) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (lead Assembly author), with Gov. Gavin Newsom, who signed the measure onto the ballot June 25, 2026.
On the ballot because: The legislature passed SB 417 by the required two-thirds vote and the governor signed it. Bond acts must go to the voters. The Senate concurred twenty-nine to two on June 25, 2026.
Full legal text: SB 417, California Legislative Information (leginfo) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office ballot analysis, Proposition 1 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 1 asks California voters for permission to borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds, with the money directed at affordable housing and veteran homeownership. It is a general obligation bond measure, which is the standard way the state borrows for long-lived investments and pays the money back over time out of the annual budget—requiring higher tax revenues or lower spending on other items.
The measure splits into two very different pieces. The larger piece is $10 billion in general obligation bonds for what it calls affordable housing programs (and what detractors call “subsidized” housing programs). That money would refill the state’s main housing accounts, most of which have spent down the funds from the last housing bond, 2018’s Proposition 1. The bill directs $5.1 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program that finances rental construction, with another $1.15 billion inside that program reserved for housing tied to homelessness and social programs aimed at homelessness. Smaller amounts go to homeownership help, farmworker housing, tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure that supports new residential building.
The smaller piece is $1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program, which offers below-market mortgages to veterans. This piece matters for how voters should read the price tag. CalVet loans are mostly repaid by the veterans who take them out, so this portion is designed to carry its own cost rather than fall on the general fund. The headline number is $11.25 billion, but the part that taxpayers repay is the $10 billion housing bond.
2. The legal language
Full text: SB 417, “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026)
Key language:
“Bonds in the total amount of ten billion dollars ($10,000,000,000), exclusive of refunding bonds issued pursuant to Section 54076, or so much thereof as is necessary as determined by the committee, are hereby authorized to be issued and sold.”
What it amends: Adds Part 16.1 (commencing with Section 54050) to Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, which houses the affordable housing programs, and Article 5ab (commencing with Section 998.750) to the Military and Veterans Code, which authorizes the CalVet loan bonds. Because a bond act is enacted by the voters, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own, though it does set the program rules that govern how the money is spent.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who authored it? Authored by Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, backed by Governor Newsom and a large roster of Democratic coauthors, along with a coalition of housing developers, labor, and veterans’ groups who would receive the subsidies. The named opposition is a small number of Republican legislators and free-market groups such as the Pacific Research Institute.The bond passed with almost no Republican support, and the Senate concurrence vote was twenty-nine to two.
What does it do? Authorization to sell $11.25 billion in bonds: roughly $10 billion in general obligation bonds for affordable rental housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure, plus $1.25 billion in revenue bonds for CalVet home loans.
Where does it apply? Statewide. The money flows through existing state housing programs administered chiefly by the Department of Housing and Community Development and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
When would it take effect? Decided on the November 3, 2026, ballot. If approved, the state would sell the bonds over several years as projects come online and repay them over roughly twenty-five years.
Why did supporters put it on the ballot? Supporters point to California’s housing affordability and homelessness crisis and argue the state needs a dedicated capital source because prior bond money is nearly gone. Their stated goals are to build and preserve “affordable” homes, expand homeownership for lower-income residents and veterans, and leverage federal and private dollars.
4. Trade-offs
A bond is first and last a borrowing and subsequent repayment decision. The Legislative Analyst estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing portion would cost the general fund roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years. That is money committed to interest and principal for a quarter century, unavailable for schools, healthcare, or anything else, and locked in regardless of the state’s budget condition in any given year. California’s independent analyst frames the real cost plainly. Paying for these programs with borrowed money rather than cash on hand costs the state about 15 percent more after adjusting for inflation. In nominal dollars the gap is larger. One outside estimate puts total repayment near $17.4 billion, of which about $7.4 billion is interest, so a large share of every repayment dollar buys interest rather than housing. Either way, the honest statement is that borrowing is not free, and the premium is the price of building now instead of later.
The case for paying that premium is not weak, and voters should weigh it fairly. Housing is a long-lived asset, and financing long-lived assets with long-term debt is a defensible match, the same logic a family uses for a mortgage. The programs the bond refills are largely spent out, so the practical alternative is not cheaper cash, it is less housing built during a severe shortage. Supporters also argue that each state dollar pulls in roughly four dollars of federal tax credits, local funds, and private capital, which means the state’s borrowing is not the whole capital stack but a match that unlocks the rest.
Voters should also consider the usefulness of government-provided and allocated so-called affordable housing. The record of massive cost overruns (hundreds of thousands of dollars for tiny homeless units) is not encouraging. Affordable housing is really taxpayer-subsidized housing. When it is allocated to people with low incomes, people have to win lotteries and then face the danger of losing their housing subsidies if they earn more money or have an opportunity to get a better job if they move. It can lock people into poverty. The state and cities already pour large amounts into so-called affordable housing directly, and this plan would force developers to create such housing in return for permission to build market-rate housing. Voters should consider if more is needed. Finally, the central source of the housing affordability crisis is the state’s and cities’ limitations on private housing construction. Creating more government-subsidized and politically allocated housing instead of simply allowing people to build houses would, arguably, only make the crisis worse.
That is the trade-off. On one side, a $500 million to $600 million annual claim on the budget for twenty-five years and an inflation-adjusted premium of about 15 percent for borrowing rather than paying cash. On the other side, potentially tens of thousands of affordable and supportive homes financed during a housing emergency, with outside money leveraged on top, but potentially more boondoggles. This bond does nothing to cut the existing red tape around building “affordable” housing. The sharper question is not whether housing is worth building. It is whether a general obligation bond, repaid by all taxpayers over a generation, to fund government provision and allocation of more housing, is the right tool, or whether the same goal should compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against everything else each year.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Refills the state’s main affordable housing accounts, most of which have drained the 2018 bond funds, so the money would sustain construction during a severe shortage.
Directs the largest share, $5.1 billion, to the Multifamily Housing Program, with $1.15 billion for supportive housing aimed at homelessness.
Matches long-term debt to a long-lived asset, the same financing logic used for other capital investments.
Reportedly leverages roughly four dollars of federal, local, and private capital for each state dollar, expanding the total built.
Expands homeownership at little direct taxpayer cost since the $1.25 billion CalVet portion is designed to be repaid by veteran borrowers, not the general fund.
Potential risks
Commits the general fund to roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years, money unavailable for other priorities regardless of the state’s fiscal condition.
Produces borrowing costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying for the same programs with cash, and a large share of nominal repayment is interest.
Arrives as California faces budget deficits, adding a fixed cost on top of existing bond debt already near $6 billion a year in debt service.
Says nothing about the permitting, land, and labor costs that drive California’s high per-unit building costs, so more money does not guarantee proportionally more units.
Accepts that the leverage and unit-count claims come largely from proponents and assumes federal credits and local matches materialize as projected.
Builds housing that by definition does not pay for itself, leading people to live where they do not want to live and trapping them away from economic opportunity. There’s a potential for great waste.
6. Open questions
What will each subsidized unit actually cost to build with this money, and how many homes will $10 billion buy at current California construction costs?
Who will get them and how?
Does bond financing add enough housing sooner to justify the inflation-adjusted premium over paying cash through the budget?
How firm is the “four dollars leveraged per state dollar” claim once federal credit availability and local matches are tested?
Given projected deficits, what other spending gives way when $500 million to $600 million a year is committed to debt service for twenty-five years?
How much of the money reaches new construction versus preservation and program overhead, and who tracks the units delivered?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A bond is a decision to build now and pay later, with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says borrowing for these housing programs costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying cash. Before you vote, ask whether building affordable homes during this shortage is worth that premium and a $500 million to $600 million yearly claim on the budget for the next twenty-five years.
Almost every voter wants more affordable housing. But government-provided housing is not more affordable to the state as a whole. It is only affordable to the select few recipients because taxpayers pay for it. The real question is the tool. Should this spending be locked in as bond debt that all taxpayers repay over a generation, or should it compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against schools, healthcare, and everything else each year?
Learn More About California

Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who authored it? Authored by Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, backed by Governor Newsom and a large roster of Democratic coauthors, along with a coalition of housing developers, labor, and veterans’ groups who would receive the subsidies. The named opposition is a small number of Republican legislators and free-market groups such as the Pacific Research Institute.The bond passed with almost no Republican support, and the Senate concurrence vote was twenty-nine to two.
What does it do? Authorization to sell $11.25 billion in bonds: roughly $10 billion in general obligation bonds for affordable rental housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure, plus $1.25 billion in revenue bonds for CalVet home loans.

When would it take effect? Decided on the November 3, 2026, ballot. If approved, the state would sell the bonds over several years as projects come online and repay them over roughly twenty-five years.
Why did supporters put it on the ballot? Supporters point to California’s housing affordability and homelessness crisis and argue the state needs a dedicated capital source because prior bond money is nearly gone. Their stated goals are to build and preserve “affordable” homes, expand homeownership for lower-income residents and veterans, and leverage federal and private dollars.
4. Trade-offs
A bond is first and last a borrowing and subsequent repayment decision. The Legislative Analyst estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing portion would cost the general fund roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years. That is money committed to interest and principal for a quarter century, unavailable for schools, healthcare, or anything else, and locked in regardless of the state’s budget condition in any given year. California’s independent analyst frames the real cost plainly. Paying for these programs with borrowed money rather than cash on hand costs the state about 15 percent more after adjusting for inflation. In nominal dollars the gap is larger. One outside estimate puts total repayment near $17.4 billion, of which about $7.4 billion is interest, so a large share of every repayment dollar buys interest rather than housing. Either way, the honest statement is that borrowing is not free, and the premium is the price of building now instead of later.
The case for paying that premium is not weak, and voters should weigh it fairly. Housing is a long-lived asset, and financing long-lived assets with long-term debt is a defensible match, the same logic a family uses for a mortgage. The programs the bond refills are largely spent out, so the practical alternative is not cheaper cash, it is less housing built during a severe shortage. Sponsor/proponent: Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón (lead Senate author) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (lead Assembly author), with Gov. Gavin Newsom, who signed the measure onto the ballot June 25, 2026.
On the ballot because: The legislature passed SB 417 by the required two-thirds vote and the governor signed it. Bond acts must go to the voters. The Senate concurred twenty-nine to two on June 25, 2026.
Full legal text: SB 417, California Legislative Information (leginfo) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office ballot analysis, Proposition 1 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 1 asks California voters for permission to borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds, with the money directed at affordable housing and veteran homeownership. It is a general obligation bond measure, which is the standard way the state borrows for long-lived investments and pays the money back over time out of the annual budget—requiring higher tax revenues or lower spending on other items.
The measure splits into two very different pieces. The larger piece is $10 billion in general obligation bonds for what it calls affordable housing programs (and what detractors call “subsidized” housing programs). That money would refill the state’s main housing accounts, most of which have spent down the funds from the last housing bond, 2018’s Proposition 1. The bill directs $5.1 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program that finances rental construction, with another $1.15 billion inside that program reserved for housing tied to homelessness and social programs aimed at homelessness. Smaller amounts go to homeownership help, farmworker housing, tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure that supports new residential building.
The smaller piece is $1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program, which offers below-market mortgages to veterans. This piece matters for how voters should read the price tag. CalVet loans are mostly repaid by the veterans who take them out, so this portion is designed to carry its own cost rather than fall on the general fund. The headline number is $11.25 billion, but the part that taxpayers repay is the $10 billion housing bond.
2. The legal language
Full text: SB 417, “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026)
Key language:
“Bonds in the total amount of ten billion dollars ($10,000,000,000), exclusive of refunding bonds issued pursuant to Section 54076, or so much thereof as is necessary as determined by the committee, are hereby authorized to be issued and sold.”
What it amends: Adds Part 16.1 (commencing with Section 54050) to Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, which houses the affordable housing programs, and Article 5ab (commencing with Section 998.750) to the Military and Veterans Code, which authorizes the CalVet loan bonds. Because a bond act is enacted by the voters, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own, though it does set the program rules that govern how the money is spent.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who authored it? Authored by Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, backed by Governor Newsom and a large roster of Democratic coauthors, along with a coalition of housing developers, labor, and veterans’ groups who would receive the subsidies. The named opposition is a small number of Republican legislators and free-market groups such as the Pacific Research Institute.The bond passed with almost no Republican support, and the Senate concurrence vote was twenty-nine to two.
What does it do? Authorization to sell $11.25 billion in bonds: roughly $10 billion in general obligation bonds for affordable rental housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure, plus $1.25 billion in revenue bonds for CalVet home loans.
Where does it apply? Statewide. The money flows through existing state housing programs administered chiefly by the Department of Housing and Community Development and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
When would it take effect? Decided on the November 3, 2026, ballot. If approved, the state would sell the bonds over several years as projects come online and repay them over roughly twenty-five years.
Why did supporters put it on the ballot? Supporters point to California’s housing affordability and homelessness crisis and argue the state needs a dedicated capital source because prior bond money is nearly gone. Their stated goals are to build and preserve “affordable” homes, expand homeownership for lower-income residents and veterans, and leverage federal and private dollars.
4. Trade-offs
A bond is first and last a borrowing and subsequent repayment decision. The Legislative Analyst estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing portion would cost the general fund roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years. That is money committed to interest and principal for a quarter century, unavailable for schools, healthcare, or anything else, and locked in regardless of the state’s budget condition in any given year. California’s independent analyst frames the real cost plainly. Paying for these programs with borrowed money rather than cash on hand costs the state about 15 percent more after adjusting for inflation. In nominal dollars the gap is larger. One outside estimate puts total repayment near $17.4 billion, of which about $7.4 billion is interest, so a large share of every repayment dollar buys interest rather than housing. Either way, the honest statement is that borrowing is not free, and the premium is the price of building now instead of later.
The case for paying that premium is not weak, and voters should weigh it fairly. Housing is a long-lived asset, and financing long-lived assets with long-term debt is a defensible match, the same logic a family uses for a mortgage. The programs the bond refills are largely spent out, so the practical alternative is not cheaper cash, it is less housing built during a severe shortage. Supporters also argue that each state dollar pulls in roughly four dollars of federal tax credits, local funds, and private capital, which means the state’s borrowing is not the whole capital stack but a match that unlocks the rest.
Voters should also consider the usefulness of government-provided and allocated so-called affordable housing. The record of massive cost overruns (hundreds of thousands of dollars for tiny homeless units) is not encouraging. Affordable housing is really taxpayer-subsidized housing. When it is allocated to people with low incomes, people have to win lotteries and then face the danger of losing their housing subsidies if they earn more money or have an opportunity to get a better job if they move. It can lock people into poverty. The state and cities already pour large amounts into so-called affordable housing directly, and this plan would force developers to create such housing in return for permission to build market-rate housing. Voters should consider if more is needed. Finally, the central source of the housing affordability crisis is the state’s and cities’ limitations on private housing construction. Creating more government-subsidized and politically allocated housing instead of simply allowing people to build houses would, arguably, only make the crisis worse.
That is the trade-off. On one side, a $500 million to $600 million annual claim on the budget for twenty-five years and an inflation-adjusted premium of about 15 percent for borrowing rather than paying cash. On the other side, potentially tens of thousands of affordable and supportive homes financed during a housing emergency, with outside money leveraged on top, but potentially more boondoggles. This bond does nothing to cut the existing red tape around building “affordable” housing. The sharper question is not whether housing is worth building. It is whether a general obligation bond, repaid by all taxpayers over a generation, to fund government provision and allocation of more housing, is the right tool, or whether the same goal should compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against everything else each year.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Refills the state’s main affordable housing accounts, most of which have drained the 2018 bond funds, so the money would sustain construction during a severe shortage.
Directs the largest share, $5.1 billion, to the Multifamily Housing Program, with $1.15 billion for supportive housing aimed at homelessness.
Matches long-term debt to a long-lived asset, the same financing logic used for other capital investments.
Reportedly leverages roughly four dollars of federal, local, and private capital for each state dollar, expanding the total built.
Expands homeownership at little direct taxpayer cost since the $1.25 billion CalVet portion is designed to be repaid by veteran borrowers, not the general fund.
Potential risks
Commits the general fund to roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years, money unavailable for other priorities regardless of the state’s fiscal condition.
Produces borrowing costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying for the same programs with cash, and a large share of nominal repayment is interest.
Arrives as California faces budget deficits, adding a fixed cost on top of existing bond debt already near $6 billion a year in debt service.
Says nothing about the permitting, land, and labor costs that drive California’s high per-unit building costs, so more money does not guarantee proportionally more units.
Accepts that the leverage and unit-count claims come largely from proponents and assumes federal credits and local matches materialize as projected.
Builds housing that by definition does not pay for itself, leading people to live where they do not want to live and trapping them away from economic opportunity. There’s a potential for great waste.
6. Open questions
What will each subsidized unit actually cost to build with this money, and how many homes will $10 billion buy at current California construction costs?
Who will get them and how?
Does bond financing add enough housing sooner to justify the inflation-adjusted premium over paying cash through the budget?
How firm is the “four dollars leveraged per state dollar” claim once federal credit availability and local matches are tested?
Given projected deficits, what other spending gives way when $500 million to $600 million a year is committed to debt service for twenty-five years?
How much of the money reaches new construction versus preservation and program overhead, and who tracks the units delivered?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A bond is a decision to build now and pay later, with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says borrowing for these housing programs costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying cash. Before you vote, ask whether building affordable homes during this shortage is worth that premium and a $500 million to $600 million yearly claim on the budget for the next twenty-five years.
Almost every voter wants more affordable housing. But government-provided housing is not more affordable to the state as a whole. It is only affordable to the select few recipients because taxpayers pay for it. The real question is the tool. Should this spending be locked in as bond debt that all taxpayers repay over a generation, or should it compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against schools, healthcare, and everything else each year?

I'm weighing the remaining factors: the Republican Party is neutral, the endorsements are broad, and the past housing bonds have all passed. I'm also looking at the risks, like anti-debt sentiment, the $44B total on the ballot, and older voters being less supportive, while noting that the March 2024 Prop 1 passed only narrowly.

I'm trying to check how far off the polls have been on earlier California measures, starting with what PPIC found before the February 2024 Prop 1 vote, and maybe the October 2018 Prop 1 poll too. I'll look it up to calibrate the polling error, since the numbers I'm recalling feel uncertain.

The article is in future tense, so the vote hasn't happened yet, and I need to predict the outcome. The polling points clearly toward "yes": about 60% in one survey and 54% in another, with no organized opposition campaign.

I'm weighing the remaining factors: the Republican Party is neutral, the endorsements are broad, and the past housing bonds have all passed. I'm also looking at the risks, like anti-debt sentiment, the $44B total on the ballot, and older voters being less supportive, while noting that the March 2024 Prop 1 passed only narrowly.

I'm trying to check how far off the polls have been on earlier California measures, starting with what PPIC found before the February 2024 Prop 1 vote, and maybe the October 2018 Prop 1 poll too. I'll look it up to calibrate the polling error, since the numbers I'm recalling feel uncertain.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm reminding myself that the March 2024 Prop 1 was polled at 59-38 in PPIC's February survey, about three to four weeks out, yet it passed with only 50.18%. That's roughly a 9-point overstatement of the yes share, so a 60-38 PPIC result shouldn't be treated as certain. If that same error applied, Prop 1 in 2026 would land near 51.

I'm noting that the 2024 Prop 1 result landed about nine points below the poll, so the margin I'd expect is shakier than the poll suggests. The March electorate was older and more conservative, the November electorate should lean more Democratic, and the earlier measure had organized opposition that got plenty of coverage. I'm also comparing against a few past propositions, though I'm not certain of the exact PPIC numbers for those.

I'm recalling the November PPIC polls on past propositions, which were mostly within about five points of the results, while the 2024 March Prop 1 was a large miss. I'm also weighing that the 2026 electorate could lean more Democratic given midterm enthusiasm.

I'm checking the 2018 Prop 1 PPIC poll to compare, since that bond was nearly identical in structure and passed with 56.2%.

content.thinking:
I'm reminding myself that the March 2024 Prop 1 was polled at 59-38 in PPIC's February survey, about three to four weeks out, yet it passed with only 50.18%. That's roughly a 9-point overstatement of the yes share, so a 60-38 PPIC result shouldn't be treated as certain. If that same error applied, Prop 1 in 2026 would land near 51.

I'm noting that the 2024 Prop 1 result landed about nine points below the poll, so the margin I'd expect is shakier than the poll suggests. The March electorate was older and more conservative, the November electorate should lean more Democratic, and the earlier measure had organized opposition that got plenty of coverage. I'm also comparing against a few past propositions, though I'm not certain of the exact PPIC numbers for those.

I'm recalling the November PPIC polls on past propositions, which were mostly within about five points of the results, while the 2024 March Prop 1 was a large miss. I'm also weighing that the 2026 electorate could lean more Democratic given midterm enthusiasm.

I'm checking the 2018 Prop 1 PPIC poll to compare, since that bond was nearly identical in structure and passed with 56.2%.

Results of SurveyUSA Election Poll #28073
Geography: California Sponsors:

PercentagesResults of SurveyUSA Election Poll #28073 - Page 1© 2026 SurveyUSA - www.surveyusa.com
Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.
