Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

Dems Remain in Charge in California Governor and US House Races; Lead for Proposition 39 Narrows, But Support for Proposition 40 Drops:
Just over a week until votes are counted, SurveyUSA's latest statewide tracking poll for KGTV News 10 and the San Diego Union-Tribune shows no real change in 3 statewide contests, some
movement in another, and enough change in the 5th to potentially switch the outcome. Here's how it all breaks down:
Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton each fall a nominal single point in the race for Governor from our last poll one month ago, leaving Becerra just where he was in September,
22 points ahead of Hilton, 54% to 32%, with 14% of voters undecided. Hilton last month led among four demographic groups, each of which continues to give him a double-digit advantage today:
by 75 points among conservatives, by 69 points among Republicans, by 65 points among 2024 Trump voters, and by 28 points among voters who say immigration is the biggest issue facing
California. This month, Hilton adds two new groups to his column: rural voters, where he leads by a nominal single point, a 6-point switch from one month ago, when Becerra had a 5-point
advantage ; and among a newly reported group, white evangelical voters, where Hilton leads by 41. Becerra leads meaningfully, by no fewer than 7 percentage points, throughout the rest of the
state and across all demographic subgroups.
The situation is virtually identical in generic US House balloting, where 58% of likely voters tell SurveyUSA they will vote for a Democratic candidate, unchanged from last month , and 32% say they
will vote for a Republican, down a nominal and statistically insignificant point. Generic Republicans run slightly ahead of Hilton among Republican voters (76-point margin for House, 69-point
margin for Governor) and Trump voters (73 points for House, 65 points for Governor); the numbers are roughly the same, within 2-3 points, among rural voters and conservatives; Hilton runs more
strongly than generic House candidates among white evangelicals (a 15-point difference, 41 points for Hilton vs. 26 points for Republican House candidates) and among voters most focused on
immigration (28 points vs. 14 points).
Any outcome is possible in the less-followed down-ballot race for the nonpartisan Superintendent of Public Instruction position. 41% of voters are undecided here, down from 53% in September .
34% of likely voters say they will vote for Richard Barrera, a Democrat and president of the San Diego Unified School District Board of Education (up 8 points from 26% last month); 25% say they
will vote for Sonja Shaw, a Republican and president of the Chino Valley Unified School District Board of Education (up 5 points from 20%). Last month, "undecided" was ahead of both candidates
with the only exceptions being voters under age 35 and those voters most focused on housing; today, undecided is the leading choice for fewer subgroups, but still leads in most. Notably, 21% of
those who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot say they don't recall how they voted in this contest – compared to 2% in the gubernatorial and 5% in the US House races.
Turning next to ballot measures, Proposition 39 , which would require voters to show government identification in order to vote, passes today by a sub-majority 7-point margin, 49% to 42%, with
10% of likely voters undecided. That's a 3-point net dip from last month , when 'yes' led 'no' by 10 points, 48% to 38%. Opposition to ballot measures typically rises as the election nears, and with 1
in 10 voters as yet undecided, any outcome is possible here. We note that among the 20% of the electorate who tell SurveyUSA they have already returned their ballot, the measure fails by a
13-point margin, while it leads by 9 points among those who say they are certain to vote this year and by 22 among those who say they probably will vote.
Proposition 40 , which would collect a one-time tax from billionaires, was up 8 points last month , 48% to 40%, but today leads by a single nominal point, 44% to 43%, with 13% undecided. Those
who have already voted say they voted no by a 35-point margin, 65% to 30%; those who say they are certain to vote support the measure by a 7-point margin, with 47% voting yes and 40% no;
among probable voters, it's a 21-point margin for yes, 49% to 28%. Given the shift from September to October here, Proposition 40 seems likely to fail.
Reviewing net approval ratings and looking at their month-on-month change, reporting them from highest to lowest: +5: Gavin Newsom. 48% today approve and 43% disapprove of the job
Newsom is doing as Governor; that's up from +2 in September. +0: The state legislature. 40% approve, 40% disapprove. That's up from -5 last month. -40: Donald Trump. 27% approve and 67%
disapprove. Last month, Trump was at -37 – a 3-point decline. -49: Congress. 17% approve, 66% disapprove; down one point from last month. Fully crosstabbed results, including additional
questions on the economy, follow. Be sure to click the triangle-T icon where it appears to display SurveyUSA's exclusive interactive tracking graphs and see month-to-month changes broken down
by demographic subgroup and region.

California voters are casting ballots in races for governor and the state’s 52 US House seats. Four House races could be competitive, according to ratings from the Cook Political Report (https://www.cookpolitical.com/ratings). In California’s open gubernatorial race, Democrat Xavier Becerra faces Republican Steve Hilton (https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2026-steve-hilton-weekend-interview/). Bloomberg News is also tracking eight key ballot measures across the Golden State, including a one-time wealth tax on billionaires and changes to the state’s environmental quality legislation.
California voters approved a ballot measure in 2025 that allows the state (https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-02-04/supreme-court-allows-new-california-voting-map-for-midterms) to use a congressional map drawn by the legislature. The new congressional map supported by Democratic Governor Gavin Newsom is intended to increase the share of Democratic-leaning House districts.

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I'm checking whether any votes have been counted yet, and it looks like none have, so the election's outcome isn't known in these pages. I'm leaning toward "yes" as the likelier result, and I'm weighing a couple of other factors too, starting with ballot position.

I'm weighing the broader mood: most voters say the state is headed the wrong way, and Newsom's approval is only modestly positive. His weak marks on housing could make some people doubt a housing bond, though PPIC's October poll shows support rising to 60%. I'm also checking whether older voters, who split in September, moved in October, starting with the age breakdown in the October crosstabs.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).

Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.

Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.

content.thinking:
I'm checking whether any votes have been counted yet, and it looks like none have, so the election's outcome isn't known in these pages. I'm leaning toward "yes" as the likelier result, and I'm weighing a couple of other factors too, starting with ballot position.

I'm weighing the broader mood: most voters say the state is headed the wrong way, and Newsom's approval is only modestly positive. His weak marks on housing could make some people doubt a housing bond, though PPIC's October poll shows support rising to 60%. I'm also checking whether older voters, who split in September, moved in October, starting with the age breakdown in the October crosstabs.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . Forty-two percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the percentage of voters needed to approve local special taxes from a majority to two-thirds; 55 percent would vote no. 2026 California Prop 1 guide: Affordable rentals get $7.2 billion of the $11.25 billion housing bond
Prop 1’s supporters stress “no new taxes,” which is true. The General Fund would still repay $10 billion at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Here is what that money buys, and why the $1.25 billion veterans’ share costs the state nothing directly.
by
Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/author/pat/)
Updated
October 17, 2026
Link copied!
Copy failed!
California's Proposition 1 is asking voters to borrow $11.25 billion for affordable rental housing, homebuyers and veterans' home loans.
Proposition 1 would let California borrow $11.25 billion by selling general obligation bonds. Ten billion dollars would go to 11 existing state housing programs and be repaid from the General Fund, mostly to build and preserve apartments rented to low-income households, with the rest for homebuyer help, infrastructure, and farmworker, student and tribal housing. The other $1.25 billion would fund CalVet home loans, which veterans repay through their mortgage payments. The Legislative Analyst's Office puts the cost at $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years, roughly a quarter of 1% of the General Fund, and estimates the money would subsidize up to 40,000 rental units and help up to 40,000 households with homeownership. The measure creates no new tax; the debt is paid from the state's existing revenue.
The Affordable Housing Bond under Proposition 1 is sending $7.2 billion of its $11.25 billion to rental housing, led by $5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. Prop 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026, is a legislative statute (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/) placed on the ballot by SB 417, which the Legislature passed and Governor Gavin Newsom signed on June 25. It is one of 14 measures in this year's guide (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) and the third California measure numbered Proposition 1 to borrow for housing since 2018, following the $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond of 2018 and the $6.38 billion behavioral health bond voters approved by 26,223 votes in March 2024. PPIC's September survey found 55% yes and 43% no. No argument against it was filed and no opposition committee exists; the Yes side reports $7.9 million from top donors, including Airbnb, two carpenters' councils, Building a Better California and nonprofit housing developers. This explainer covers where each dollar goes, the veterans' loan bond, the Legislature's power to move money between programs, the cost, the earlier Prop 1s, the money, the argument and the polling.
2026 California propositions master guide: All 14 measures on the November 3 ballot California's November 3, 2026 ballot carries 14 propositions, from an $11.25 billion housing bond to a one-time billionaire tax. This guide covers each measure's rules, its cost according to the Legislative Analyst, who is funding both sides, and where the polls stand as ballots arrive. California Today Mac Douglass | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-propositions-master-guide/) Proposition 1 would borrow $10 billion for 11 state housing programs and $1.25 billion for veterans' home loans:
The text of the measure (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf) has two parts. The first adds Part 16.1 to the Health and Safety Code, creating the Affordable Housing Bond Act Trust Fund of 2026 and authorizing $10 billion in bonds that are "a valid and binding general obligation of the state," with "the full faith and credit of the state … pledged" to repay them. The second adds an article to the Military and Veterans Code authorizing $1.25 billion in veterans' bonds for the farm and home loan program the Department of Veterans Affairs runs under the Veterans' Farm and Home Purchase Act of 1974. Both sets of bonds are sold over time by state finance committees as programs ask for cash, so the state does not borrow the full amount at once.
Section 54054 divides the $10 billion into 11 lines, each assigned to a program already in state law. The Attorney General's summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/title-summary.htm) groups them as $5.1 billion for multifamily rental housing, $2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate or preserve affordable housing and provide supportive housing, $1.1 billion for homeownership, $1 billion for farmworker, tribal and student housing, $500 million for infrastructure and $200 million for local programs. The LAO's analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/analysis.htm) combines the first two into a single $7.2 billion for affordable multifamily housing. The summary also notes that the money can finance "housing development projects seeking federal tax credits," and the LAO expects most of it to be "used together with other government monies."
Prop 1's $7.2 billion for rental housing runs mostly through the Multifamily Housing Program:
The largest line, $5.1 billion, goes to the Department of Housing and Community Development's Multifamily Housing Program, which lends to developers of new and renovated apartments in exchange for rent limits. The LAO describes these as "low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost," with units generally reserved for low-income households "for a period of 55 years." Prop 1 adds one condition of its own: at least 10% of the assisted units in each development must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
A further $1.15 billion is set aside for supportive housing, where residents get on-site services such as mental health and substance use counseling. The administering agency must offer capitalized operating subsidy reserves for those units, money set aside up front to cover the gap between what very low-income tenants can pay and what the building costs to run. melessness, and $150 million is reserved for youth housing for current and former foster youth and homeless or at-risk young people, usable only for construction and acquisition and returned to the general program if not committed within three years.
The other two rental lines are about keeping existing housing affordable. The Portfolio Reinvestment Program gets $750 million; its statute, Health and Safety Code section 50606 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=50606), says it exists to "maintain the supply and quality of the affordable rental housing units for which there has already been a significant public investment," including older state-funded buildings whose affordability periods are ending. Another $200 million funds a new program to buy apartments with no rent restrictions and attach long-term affordability limits, "while safeguarding against the displacement of current residents."
The McClatchy editorial board, which recommends (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html) a yes vote, cites Enterprise Community Partners' count of "nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes" that are designed and approved but waiting for financing, and the California Budget & Policy Center's estimate that each state dollar draws $4 from federal, local and private sources. Those are the board's and those groups' figures; the LAO's own estimate is that the bond would subsidize "up to 40,000 multifamily rental units," with the money "used together with other government monies."
Proposition 1 puts $1.1 billion into homeownership through CalHome and CalHFA:
Two lines make up the homeownership money. The CalHome Program receives $600 million for "direct, forgivable loans" to developments with multiple ownership units, including single-family subdivisions, self-help housing where buyers help build their own homes, and manufactured homes. The California Housing Finance Agency receives $500 million for its Home Purchase Assistance Program, which state law (section 51341 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=HSC&sectionNum=51341)) aims at making homes "affordable to low- and moderate-income buyers who intend to occupy the homes as their primary residences." That money is continuously appropriated, so CalHFA can spend it without waiting for an annual budget act. The LAO says part of the homeownership money would go to first-time buyers "through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off."
This is a different kind of help from the Proposition 37 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-37-guide/) loan on the same ballot. Prop 1's homeownership money is a General Fund-backed subsidy aimed at low- and moderate-income buyers and generally deferred until sale. Prop 37 would have CalHFA sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages on new homes that buyers repay monthly, with no General Fund backing.
California’s Proposition 37 would let buyers put 3% down on a new home, with a state loan covering the other 17% Proposition 37 would let CalHFA sell $25 billion in revenue bonds and lend buyers of newly built homes up to 17% of the price, so they can put 3% down. The loan is a fixed-rate second mortgage with monthly payments. Here is who qualifies, the county price caps, the cost and who is behind it. California Today Pat Sharyon | Editor (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-37-guide/) Farmworker, student, tribal and infrastructure money makes up $1.7 billion of Proposition 1:
The Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Grant Program gets $450 million for grants and loans to build or rehabilitate housing for agricultural workers and their families, including manufactured housing for families displaced from labor camps and mobile home parks. The LAO estimates the money would fund about 2,500 farmworker units. The Infill Infrastructure Grant Program gets $500 million for the water, sewer, street and park work that high-density affordable and mixed-income projects in already built-up areas need.
The University of California and California State University split $350 million, $175 million each, for new affordable student housing under the terms of Education Code section 17201; the LAO estimates about 1,200 beds. Tribes can apply for $200 million in Tribal Housing Grant Program money "to rebuild and reconstitute their communities." The last $200 million goes to the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program for pilot projects testing "innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing," available only to local trust funds that have their own ongoing private or public revenue.
The CalVet home loan bond in Prop 1 is repaid by veterans rather than the General Fund:
The $1.25 billion veterans' portion works differently from the rest of the measure. The state sells bonds to investors and lends the money to eligible veterans to buy homes, farms or mobile homes, and the veterans' mortgage payments flow back to the fund that pays the bondholders. The LAO notes that these payments "have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state," and estimates the new money would help about 2,100 veterans.
They are still general obligation bonds. The text pledges the state's full faith and credit and requires the Director of Finance to transfer any shortfall from the General Fund, which the fund then repays with interest. It also requires an independent public accountant to survey the finances of CalVet's Division of Farm and Home Purchases every year while any of the bonds are outstanding. The last veterans' home loan bond was the $1 billion approved in 2018.
The Legislature could move Proposition 1 money between programs after voters approve it:
The split in the chart is a starting point. Section 54056 lets the Legislature amend the laws governing any of the funded programs "for the purposes of improving the efficiency and effectiveness of those programs," and states that it "may amend this chapter in order to reallocate the proceeds of bonds issued and sold pursuant to this part among the programs to which funds are to be allocated … as necessary to effectively promote the development of affordable housing in this state." A separate clause lets the Business, Consumer Services and Housing Agency, with legislative appropriation, "align or streamline" the programs "to improve efficiency and accelerate the deployment of funds," as long as spending stays within the purposes voters approved.
Unspent money also moves on its own schedule. Most lines revert to the Multifamily Housing Program if not committed by November 3, 2036; the youth housing set-aside, the $200 million acquisition program and the local pilots revert after three years. Agencies may write their own program guidelines without going through the Administrative Procedure Act, the bonds may be issued as taxable bonds and can mature in up to 35 years, and the administering agency must publish an annual report on how the bond money was invested under Health and Safety Code section 50408.
Proposition 1 would cost the General Fund $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years:
The LAO estimates repaying the $10 billion housing bond at "$500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years," or about 0.25% of the General Fund budget. "Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows," it adds, "the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has." A share of the bond money would cover the administrative costs of the agencies running the programs, and the veterans' bond carries no direct state cost as long as loan payments keep covering it.
The Voter Information Guide's Overview of State Bond Debt (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm) puts Prop 1 alongside the Proposition 38 (https://californiatoday.com/guides/elections/2026-california-proposition-38-guide/) immunology research bond as the two General Fund-supported bonds on this ballot, about $1 billion a year combined, against the roughly $6 billion a year the state already pays on about $80 billion of outstanding bonds. For scale, the LAO's analysis of the 2018 housing bond put the cost of its $3 billion General Fund portion at about $170 million a year for 35 years.
California has passed two other bonds called Proposition 1 since 2018 and both funded housing:
Voters have seen the number before. In November 2018, Proposition 1 was a $4 billion veterans and affordable housing bond built on the same template, with $3 billion for state housing programs and $1 billion for CalVet loans. It passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2018-general/sov/07-summary.pdf) with 56.2%. In March 2024, Proposition 1 was a $6.38 billion behavioral health bond, which paid for treatment facilities and $2 billion of housing for homeless people with mental health or substance use challenges, just over half of it for veterans, and also changed how the Mental Health Services Act tax is spent. It passed (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-primary/ssov/ballot-measure-summary.pdf) with 50.2%, by 26,223 votes out of more than 7.2 million. The LAO counts that 2024 measure as "the last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing."

Compiled by California Today from each election's Voter Information Guide (Legislative Analyst's analysis) and the Secretary of State's Statements of Vote. Dollar categories follow each measure's own allocation; the 2024 measure's housing money went to a single homelessness-focused program, so it is shown under rental housing.
The 2026 bond is nearly three times the size of the 2018 one, with the rental share up from $1.8 billion to $7.2 billion. It also funds lines the 2018 bond did not have, including UC and CSU student housing, tribal housing, preservation of existing affordable buildings and capitalized operating reserves for supportive housing.
SB 417 cleared the Legislature 61–7 and 29–2 on June 25, 2026:
SB 417, by Senator Monique Limón, was introduced in February 2025 and passed (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) the Senate 30–9 on January 27, 2026 with an urgency clause. The Assembly amended it on June 22 and passed it 61–7 on June 25. That same day the Senate concurred 29–2 and Governor Newsom signed it as Chapter 16 of the Statutes of 2026. As a bond act, it takes effect only if voters approve it on November 3.
CalMatters' voter guide lists "some Republican state lawmakers" as the opposition and summarizes their objections: that the bill uses veterans to build support while doing little for them, and that it borrows more for housing without addressing why housing is so expensive to build.
Proposition 1's Yes side reports $7.9 million from Airbnb, carpenters and housing developers with no opposition committee:
The Fair Political Practices Commission's top-contributor list (https://www.fppc.ca.gov/search-filings/top-10-contributors-list/november-2026-general-election/), last updated October 14, shows $7.89 million in support of Prop 1 across two committees and no opposing committee large enough to appear. The main committee, "Yes on Prop 1 Californians for Homes, Jobs and Affordability 2026," sponsored by affordable housing organizations, lists $6.8 million from its top ten: $1 million each from Airbnb, the Western States Regional Council of Carpenters' issues committee, the North Coast States Regional Council of Carpenters' PAC and Building a Better California, the Sergey Brin and John Doerr-funded committee that is also the main opponent of the billionaire tax (https://californiatoday.com/news/elections/what-exactly-is-the-california-billionaire-tax/); $700,000 from a second Yes committee sponsored by NPH Action Fund; $500,000 each from Anthropic PBC and Pacific West Communities of Idaho; $400,000 from Housing Trust Silicon Valley; and $350,000 each from Eden Housing and MidPen Housing. The NPH committee lists $1.09 million of its own, mostly from its sponsor's issues committee, plus $150,000 each from Scott D. Cook and H. Signe Ostby. Because the NPH committee's $700,000 transfer appears on both lists, the FPPC's combined figure counts that money twice.
The Secretary of State's contribution tally (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-1-sb-417-limon-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond-act-2026-ch-16-2026), which counts all contributions rather than only top donors and runs through October 6, shows $12.8 million across three Yes committees, including a third formed by the California Homeless and Housing Coalition Action Fund, and "No committees identified" in opposition.
The argument for Prop 1 promises no new taxes and no argument against was filed:
The argument in favor (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/arguments-rebuttals.htm), signed by Anni Chung of Self-Help for the Elderly, Jeffery Freitas of the California Federation of Teachers and John H. Ing of US Vets, is headed "Affordable homes for veterans, seniors, people with disabilities and working families—without raising taxes." It says "more than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California's state budget goes to housing," that the CalVet Home Loan Program "has already helped almost a million veterans and their families," and that the bond "unlocks federal matching funds." It quotes Michael Blecker of the California Association of Veteran Service Agencies: "After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home." The guide's index lists US Vets, the California Federation of Teachers, Self-Help for the Elderly, Habitat for Humanity California and the California Alliance of Child and Family Services as supporters.
The page for the argument against reads: "NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 1 WAS SUBMITTED." The guide notes that arguments "have not been checked for accuracy by any official agency."
Proposition 1 leads 55% to 43% with Newsom, Becerra and Democrats in support and editorial boards split:
PPIC's September survey (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0926.pdf) of likely voters, fielded September 4–10, found 55% yes, 43% no and 2% undecided. Democrats back it 75% to 23% and independents 56% to 41%, while Republicans oppose it 79% to 19%. Renters support it 72% to 27%, and homeowners split evenly at 49% each. Support falls with age and income: voters under 35 back it 69% to 29% and those 55 and older oppose it 51% to 46%, while households earning under $40,000 back it 78% to 18% and those earning $100,000 or more split 49% to 49%. Five percent named it the measure they are most interested in. UC Berkeley's September poll did not ask about it, and PPIC's October survey had not been released as of October 18.
Governor Newsom announced his support on October 9 as part of his ballot slate, and Xavier Becerra listed (https://www.xavierbecerra2026.com/?p=551) "YES on Prop 1" among his positions on July 31. The California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf) supports it and the California Republican Party (https://cagop.org/endorsements/) is neutral, one of two measures on which it takes no side; the other is Proposition 37. CalMatters also lists the California Apartment Association and AFL-CIO California among supporters.
The McClatchy board recommends yes and asks the state to use the bond to learn "precisely why affordable housing costs what it does," calling for standardized cost data on every funded project and a public dashboard of money awarded and spent, units built and cost per unit. The San Francisco Chronicle recommends yes, according to CalMatters' roster (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) of editorials. The Orange County Register recommends (https://www.ocregister.com/2026/09/23/endorsement-no-on-prop-1-more-debt-wont-fix-californias-housing-shortage/) no under the headline "More debt won't fix California's housing shortage," opening: "Is the answer to California's housing crisis more bonds and more debt? Of course not."
Proposition 1 after November 3 would start a decade of housing bond awards:
If Prop 1 passes, the Housing Finance Committee and the Veterans' Finance Committee would decide when to sell bonds as HCD, CalHFA and CalVet ask for cash, and the money would reach projects through each program's competitive rounds over several years; most lines have until November 3, 2036 to be committed before reverting to the Multifamily Housing Program. The Legislature could reshuffle the split between programs in later budget years, and each year's awards would appear in the agencies' annual bond reports. If it fails, the state's most recent housing bond money remains the 2024 measure's $2 billion for homelessness-focused housing and the only other homeownership measure on this ballot is Proposition 37's revenue-bond loan program.

Photo by Damian Dovarganes, AP Photo In summary Supporters say California desperately needs money to fund housing construction and make a dent in its homelessness and affordability crisis. Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-polls-22503108.php
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging.
In early October, a Politico poll found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop.

California’s proposed billionaires tax is losing support days before Election Day, according to the second major independent poll released this week.
Thursday’s poll by the Institute of Governmental Studies at UC Berkeley found 42% of likely voters in favor of Proposition 40 and 50% opposed, with 8% undecided.
In a mid-September Berkeley IGS poll, 45% of likely voters favored Proposition 40, while 42% were opposed and 13% were undecided.
It would need majority support to pass.
The measure would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the wealth of California billionaires.
A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.
Proposition 41 had support from 38% of likely voters while 47% were opposed and 16% were undecided, compared to IGS’ mid-September poll in which 37% were in favor, 33% opposed and 30% undecided.
Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass.

Sen. Bernie Sanders speaks at a campaign rally in support of California Proposition 40 in Los Angeles, Monday, Oct. 5, 2026. | Jae C. Hong/AP
DOWNWARD ARC — Where a campaign stands matters less than where it’s headed — and less than a week from the election, major ballot initiatives are losing ground.
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects. Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California (http://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure. But Prop 45 also plunged underwater. Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
Both measures eroded as opponents assailed their weak spots. Critics of Prop 45, which would change California’s environmental review law, have warned the measure could expedite the building of fossil fuel infrastructure and increasingly unpopular data centers. Opponents of the wealth tax have argued it could eventually be expanded to hit working Californians. Supporters disputed both claims.
PROP 3 HOLDS — The wealth tax’s slide in the polls hasn’t extended to Proposition 3, which would make permanent an existing tax on top earners to fund education. Support for that measure held steady at 58%, a result that may ease union proponents’ fears that opposition to Proposition 40 could spill over to Prop 3.
Those divergent trendlines reflected starkly different political and financial realities. The Prop 3 campaign has raised more than $80 million and faced no funded opposition; the wealth tax effort has operated on a shoestring budget as billionaires spend hundreds of millions of dollars against it. Democrats are largely unified behind Prop 3, while Prop 40 has been extraordinarily divisive within the party.
Prop 40 was not the only SEIU-UHW-championed measure to backslide as opponents piled on. Support for Proposition 44, which would regulate clinics, shrank to just 25% in the face of a $44 million health care industry counteroffensive. In both cases, SEIU-UHW spent millions on qualification but has not followed up with a comparable advertising campaign.
Two billionaire-funded measures designed to torpedo Prop 40 were also on the bubble amid tightening polling: Proposition 41 declined from a 51-44 majority in September to 48-49 this month, and Proposition 42 went from 54-43 to 51-47. Wealthy backers have largely focused on 42, pouring some $65 million into the campaign this month. But the rest of the ballot is looking increasingly predictable as campaigns either held steady or saw polling gaps expand.
THE REST OF THE BALLOT — Voters broadly support two housing bonds (Proposition 1 and Proposition 37), an expansion of the state’s “rainy day” reserve fund (Proposition 2), and an immunology research bond (Proposition 38). A voter ID measure (Proposition 39) and an initiative making it harder to raise local taxes (Proposition 43) are both trailing by double-digit margins. And two measures to institute public election financing (Proposition 4) and overhaul recalls (Proposition 5) remain below majority support despite creeping up to 45%.
